Predicted active: South Asian and Middle-Eastern personal names and places and non-Western brands/currencies (Abdul 2.7, Saurabh 2.0, Anil 1.9, Rahul 1.5, Deepak 1.4, Mumbai, Karachi, Beijing, Xiaomi 1.6, Alibaba 1.2, rupee 0.9, yuan/yen 0.5), religious vocabulary of any faith (shrine 1.8, ashram 1.6, mosque 1.3, monastery 1.1, church 0.8, rabbi 1.6, imam 1.6, monk 1.6, priest 1.0, Hindu 1.5, Muslim 1.0, Quran 1.1), and the vocabulary of irregular armed conflict (insurgent 2.3, militant 2.2, rebel 2.1, terrorist 2.1, guerrilla 2.0, martyrdom 1.9, jihad 1.6); predicted inactive on everyday English nouns, Anglophone names and Western cities, household money words and Western secular institutions (John -0.1, David -0.1, London -0.2, window -0.1, kitchen -0.1, money 0.0, dollar -0.1, salary 0.2, budget 0.1, senator 0.0, governor 0.0, senate -0.1, court 0.1) and on invented or merely Western-rare word forms (Blorfen 0.1, Zarquon -0.1, Bartholomew -0.1, sesquipedalian -0.1), so rarity or token identity alone does not label a span. The bus left the valley floor before dawn, climbing through switchbacks of pine and loose shale while the driver hummed along to a crackling radio. At the third checkpoint a guard waved us through with a bored flick of his wrist, and the old woman beside me, a bundle of turnips in her lap, fell asleep against the window. Rain came and went. The mountains did not.

By noon we had stopped twice, once for fuel and once because a truck had shed its load across both lanes and the drivers stood around it in the drizzle. I bought a bag of oranges from a boy at the roadside; they were small and green and sweeter than any orange I have eaten since. The road climbed again, the radio lost its signal, and the driver sang instead.

A woman across the aisle told me, in careful English, that her son worked at a hotel in the city, that the hotel had a swimming pool, and that this was a source of great pride and also of worry, because the son had recently bought a motorcycle. She showed me a photograph of the motorcycle. It was red. She asked whether I had children, and when I said no she nodded the way people do when they are deciding whether to be sorry for you.

It is difficult to describe arriving somewhere you have only read about, especially when the reading was done in a library thousands of miles away, between shifts at a job you have since quit. The town announced itself slowly: first the smell of woodsmoke, then a row of whitewashed shops with their shutters half raised, then the flat bronze note of a gong struck out of sight. Children ran alongside the bus, and their laughter had the sharpness of a place where the air is thin.

The road turned east and for a while the only thing outside the window was a wall of cloud. The driver slowed at a bend where men were repairing the surface with shovels and a barrel of tar. Nobody spoke. The woman with the turnips woke, looked around, and slept again. I counted the power lines between two poles and lost count after forty, and then the cloud thinned and the town appeared below us, grey roofs stacked against the slope.

The monastery above Lhasa sat at the top of the hill, its walls the color of old bone. We removed our shoes at the outer gate and kept our voices low. A young monk with a shaved head led us through courtyards where light fell in long rectangles. Butter lamps burned in the main hall, and the smell stayed in my coat for days. Old thangkas hung in the gloom, their gold flaking like dead leaves.

That night I lay awake listening to rain on a tin roof, and in the morning the bus would leave again, and the hill and the butter lamps would go back to being words in a notebook.
